title: Module 11: Masonry, lintels and existing building alterations
shortTitle: Masonry, lintels and existing building alterations
whyItMatters: Forming a new opening in an existing load-bearing masonry wall is one of the most common UK engineering tasks, and where temporary works (needling, propping, sequencing) and permanent works (beam, bearings, padstones, piers, foundations, lateral restraint) are inseparable.
introduction: Covers masonry units (clay bricks, concrete blocks, stone), mortar designations, solid vs cavity wall behaviour, compression-dominated resistance and low tensile strength, concentrated bearing loads and padstone design, wall slenderness and lateral floor/roof restraint, lintels and arching action, movement joints and cracking diagnosis, existing building survey uncertainty, temporary needling/propping sequences, and why "sizing the steel beam" alone is never a complete alteration design (Project 11.1).
objectives: Understand how unit strength, mortar strength, slenderness, and eccentricity govern masonry compressive resistance.
Check concentrated bearing stresses beneath lintels/beams and design padstones to spread loads safely into masonry piers.
Execute the 10-element whole-system assessment for forming a new opening in an existing load-bearing wall, including temporary propping and construction sequencing (Project 11.1).
learningGate: Explain clearly why "sizing the steel beam" alone is NOT a complete alteration design.,Account systematically for all 10 system elements: (1) beam, (2) bearings, (3) wall/pier capacity, (4) padstone, (5) support below, (6) foundations, (7) lateral restraint, (8) temporary works, (9) survey uncertainty, and (10) construction sequence.

questions.learningObjective: Understand the physical role of mortar in load-bearing masonry
questions.prompt: Why should structural mortar generally be slightly weaker and more deformable than the masonry units (bricks or blocks) it beds together?
options: Because bricks have zero compressive strength and mortar carries 100% of the vertical load, assuming that it redistributes the peak hogging bending moment into the adjacent midspan zone through rigid-plastic hinge rotation without requiring supplementary lateral-torsional restraint, web stiffeners, or ductile rotation capacity at the support interface
Because mortar acts as high-strength tensile glue stronger than steel

Mortar beds out surface irregularities between units to distribute compressive stress evenly, and allows slight thermal/moisture movement to be accommodated by micro-cracking in the sacrificial joints rather than fracturing the bricks themselves

It eliminates vertical shear deformation across the web depth by forcing the neutral axis to remain coincident with the geometric centroid of the uncracked transformed section throughout both construction and permanent service stages
questions.explanation: Using overly dense, rigid cement mortar on soft historic bricks traps moisture and forces thermal/settlement cracks right through the bricks. Engineering synthesis for "Understand the physical role of mortar in load-bearing masonry": always trace the complete load path from point of application to the foundations, ensure compatibility between analysis boundary assumptions and physical site detailing, and verify against BS EN 1996-1-1:2005+A1 (Eurocode 6: Masonry Structures) & BS 5975 Temporary Needling.

questions.learningObjective: Understand the role of cavity wall ties and the hazard of wall-tie corrosion
questions.prompt: In a traditional two-leaf masonry cavity wall where the floors and roof sit only on the 100 mm inner leaf, what is the structural purpose of the metal cavity wall ties connecting the inner and outer leaves?
questions.assumptions: Connects cavity wall mechanics to defect recognition.
options: They transfer 100% of the roof gravity dead load into the foundation soil directly
They prevent water from touching the outer face of the building

The design substitutes the characteristic 95th-percentile material strength in place of the 5th-percentile characteristic strength and omits the combination factor ψ_0 when superimpose-combining independent variable wind and imposed floor actions

They tie the unrestrained outer leaf to the laterally restrained inner leaf so both leaves share horizontal wind loads and increase the effective thickness (and reduce the slenderness) of the wall against buckling
questions.explanation: When older mild-steel wall ties corrode, the outer leaf loses its lateral tie to the inner leaf (becoming dangerously slender under wind suction) and expansive rust causes regular horizontal bed-joint cracking every ~450 mm!

questions.learningObjective: Understand why floor joists running parallel to a masonry wall require restraint straps
questions.prompt: When timber floor joists span ONTO a masonry wall, the joist bearings help restrain the wall horizontally. What happens along the perpendicular flank walls where the floor joists run PARALLEL to the wall without touching it?
options: Unless metal tension restraint straps (with solid timber nogging/blocking between the first 3 joists) are installed at regular intervals, the flank wall receives zero lateral restraint at floor level and spans vertically across two full storeys (doubling its slenderness and buckling risk)

Parallel joists restrain the wall by magnetic attraction across the air gap, assuming that by applying the unfactored characteristic Serviceability Limit State action combination directly to the gross cross-sectional area without accounting for partial material safety factors.

By assuming a uniform linear-elastic stress distribution across the gross flange and web elements while neglecting rotational restraint compatibility, eccentric shear-centre load introduction, and shear-lag effects at the support boundaries

By taking the mean 50th-percentile material stiffness modulus together with a fully fixed rotational boundary condition at both ends, thereby ignoring connection flexibility, long-term creep deformation, and differential support settlement under sustained gravity loading
questions.explanation: Missing lateral restraint straps on flank walls parallel to joists is one of the most frequent structural defects found in domestic surveys. questions.learningObjective: Calculate dispersed width of a concentrated load at foundation level
questions.prompt: A padstone of length 300 mm sits at a height of 2.4 m above the top of a strip foundation in a continuous solid wall (with no openings below the padstone). Assuming the concentrated reaction disperses downwards through the brickwork at an angle of 30° to the vertical (i.e. 60° to the horizontal, so horizontal spread on each side is 2,400 × tan 30° = 1,386 mm) when not cut off by a wall end, what would be the total dispersed length (in m, to 2 decimal places) if the padstone sits right at the end corner of the wall (so it can only disperse to ONE side)?
questions.assumptions: Crucial geometry check: a bearing near the end of a wall or next to a doorway cannot disperse past the free vertical edge!
questions.explanation: Because the padstone is at the end of the wall, dispersion can only occur in one direction along the wall: L_disp = 0.30 m + (2.4 m × tan 30°) = 0.30 + 1.3856 = 1.6856 m ≈ 1.69 m.

questions.learningObjective: Identify when the "45°/60° arching triangle" assumption over a lintel is INVALID
questions.prompt: For small window lintels in a tall uninterrupted masonry wall, engineers sometimes take only a triangle of brickwork above the opening on the assumption that the wall above arches around the triangle. When is this arching-triangle assumption completely INVALID and unsafe?
questions.assumptions: Prevents gross under-estimation of alteration beam loads.
options: Because the maximum principal tensile stress under pure shear equals the uniaxial yield strength according to the Rankine maximum normal stress hypothesis, which governs brittle fracture in unreinforced cast iron and uncracked plain concrete elements rather than ductile structural steel when evaluated under unfactored serviceability actions across the gross cross-section without partial safety factors or second-order geometric slenderness reductions

When there is insufficient uninterrupted masonry height above the lintel to form an arch, when there are window/door openings in the wall above, when floor or roof joists bear within or just above the zone, or when the piers at the ends of the opening are too narrow to resist the horizontal arch thrust

Because the elastic shear modulus G is related to Young’s modulus E by G = E / [2(1 + ν)], which introduces a Poisson’s ratio reduction factor across the web depth whenever transverse direct stresses are neglected in simple beam theory
Arching always reduces all floor and roof loads to zero
questions.explanation: In domestic alterations (such as knocking out a ground-floor wall under first-floor joists and upper windows), arching cannot be relied upon and the full tributary height of walls, floors, and roof must be taken!

questions.prompt: An engineer needs a 600 mm long bearing on weak masonry for a 100 mm wide steel beam sitting at the centre of the bearing, and specifies a 600 mm long × 65 mm high unreinforced concrete brick as a "padstone". Why will this fail to distribute the load over the 600 mm length?

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish clay brickwork vs concrete blockwork moisture movement
questions.prompt: How does the long-term moisture movement of fired clay brickwork differ from that of concrete blockwork (or calcium silicate bricks), and why are vertical movement joints needed?

Neither material changes length with moisture or temperature
Movement joints are used to transfer bending moments across walls

questions.learningObjective: Calculate increased line load on a remaining masonry pier after forming an opening (Project 11.1)
questions.prompt: Before alteration, a solid masonry wall carried a uniform ULS vertical line load of w = 30 kN/m along its entire length (so a 0.6 m wide section carried 30 × 0.6 = 18 kN). A 3.4 m wide opening is now cut beside a 0.6 m remaining masonry pier, so the new lintel transfers half of the 3.4 m opening load (1.7 m × 30 kN/m = 51 kN) onto that 0.6 m pier in addition to the pier’s own direct load (18 kN). What is the new average ULS vertical force per metre run (in kN/m) at the base of the 0.6 m pier?
questions.assumptions: Shows vividly why both the remaining masonry pier AND the existing strip foundation beneath that pier must be checked!
questions.explanation: Total vertical force on the 0.6 m pier = 18 kN (direct) + 51 kN (from beam reaction) = 69 kN. Average force per metre run of the 0.6 m pier = 69 kN / 0.6 m = 115 kN/m (nearly 4 times the original 30 kN/m!).

questions.prompt: Which construction sequence is required when forming a new opening in a load-bearing wall supporting first-floor joists and an upper-storey brick wall?
